title: Surprisal Theory is Tautological (without Rational Grounding)
abstract: Surprisal theory holds that the human processing difficulty of a linguistic unit in context is an affine function of its surprisal under some language model. I argue this claim is a tautology without further constraint: for any non-negative difficulty measure over units in context, there exists a language model whose surprisal is an affine function of it under mild technical conditions. Therefore, because any pattern of difficulty is consistent with some language model, without an additional constraint on the language model, surprisal theory makes no falsifiable predictions. The tautology was long obscured by an assumption implicit in two decades of psycholinguistic work---that the relevant language model is the distribution that generated the training corpus, so that improving corpus fit improves predictions of human behavior. Recent empirical work has undermined this assumption, demonstrating that better corpus models can be worse predictors of processing difficulty. I conclude that breaking the tautology requires a rationalist intervention, i.e., the relevant language model must be derived from a non-empirically motivated model of the comprehender, which could be based on, for instance, memory constraints or processing goals, and that, thus, does not depend on the behavioral data surprisal theory is meant to explain.

A foundational observation in psycholinguistics is that human language comprehension is incremental , i.e., comprehenders do not wait for a complete utterance before beginning to interpret it, but instead build and update their representations unit by unit as the input unfolds (Altmann and Kamide, 1999 ; Tanenhaus et al., 1995 ) . 3 3 3 Incrementality is not absolute: eye-tracking reveals regressive saccades in which readers revisit earlier material (Wilcox et al., 2024 ) , and late measures such as go-past time aggregate processing across multiple fixations (Boston et al., 2008 ; Demberg and Keller, 2008 ) . Nonetheless, the dominant empirical pattern is strongly left-to-right, and the standard modeling assumption in the surprisal literature is that difficulty at position t t depends on 𝒖 < t {\boldsymbol{u}}_{<t} alone. I adopt this assumption throughout; extending the framework to account for regressions is an open problem. This fact has deep consequences for how one theorizes about processing. If comprehension proceeds incrementally, then the total effort of understanding an utterance 𝒖 = u 1 ​ ⋯ ​ u T {\boldsymbol{u}}={u}_{1}\cdots{u}_{{T}} naturally decomposes into a series of per-step costs, one for each unit integrated into the evolving representation. Incrementality thus motivates the central theoretical primitive of this paper: the processing difficulty d ​ ( u t ∣ 𝒖 < t ) ≥ 0 {\mathrm{d}}({u}_{t}\mid{\boldsymbol{u}}_{<t})\geq 0 , a non-negative function that quantifies the effort a comprehender expends to integrate unit u t {u}_{t} given the preceding context 𝒖 < t = def u 1 ​ ⋯ ​ u t − 1 {\boldsymbol{u}}_{<t}\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{def}}}{{=}}}{u}_{1}\cdots{u}_{t-1} ; 4 4 4 The construct d {\mathrm{d}} is agnostic about the source of the processing effort: it subsumes prediction disconfirmation, the cost of integrating u t {u}_{t} into the evolving representation, and any reanalysis of earlier material that u t {u}_{t} triggers. Because reanalysis at position t t is initiated by observing u t {u}_{t} in context 𝒖 < t {\boldsymbol{u}}_{<t} , its cost remains a function of the pair ( u t , 𝒖 < t ) ({u}_{t},{\boldsymbol{u}}_{<t}) and is therefore representable by d {\mathrm{d}} ; indeed, under Levy ’s ( 2008 ) resource-reallocation interpretation, reanalysis costs are part of what surprisal is meant to quantify. the notation is formally introduced in § ˜ 2 . 5 5 5 I treat d {\mathrm{d}} as a function of the linguistic unit and its context alone, abstracting over reader identity, reader state, and presentation modality. This follows the standard linear mixed-effects regression framework used in psycholinguistics (Smith and Levy, 2013 ; Goodkind and Bicknell, 2018 ) , which decomposes observed reading times into a surprisal-driven component shared across readers, control predictors (word length, frequency, position), reader-specific random intercepts, and residual noise. Under this decomposition, the string-specific difficulty captured by surprisal is the same for all readers; reader-specific variation is absorbed into the random effects. If d {\mathrm{d}} were instead reader-specific, the tautology construction in Eq. 2 would produce a different language model for each reader—but surprisal theory posits a single language model shared across readers, which is itself a testable constraint that the present argument does not exploit. In practice, processing difficulty is operationalized through a variety of behavioral and neural measures—self-paced reading times, eye-tracking fixation durations, and event-related potentials, inter alia —and a successful theory of sentence processing must explain its variation across positions and contexts. However, for the exposition of this paper, I abstract away from specific operationalizations with the construct d {\mathrm{d}} . 1.1 Surprisal Theory Surprisal theory (Hale, 2001 ; Levy, 2008 ) is a widely adopted information-theoretic framework for prediction-based processing (Kuperberg and Jaeger, 2016 ) in psycholinguistics that offers a particularly elegant account of incremental processing. It claims that processing difficulty is an affine function of the contextual surprisal of the unit under some language model q {q} (Shain et al., 2024 ) ; 6 6 6 Shain et al. ( 2024 ) provide large-scale evidence that the relationship between word predictability and reading time is linear in log-probability—i.e., that the affine form in Eq. 1 is a better fit than alternatives such as a logarithmic or power-law relationship in raw probability. The affine formulation is important for my tautology argument: the construction in Eq. 2 yields a = 1 a=1 and a context-dependent intercept b = − log ⁡ Z ​ ( 𝒖 < t ) b=-\log Z({\boldsymbol{u}}_{<t}) , which is exactly the affine form. This paper argues that, in its current conceptualization, surprisal theory is not falsifiable (Popper, 1959 ) without constraints that go beyond current practice and, moreover, tautological. Because the theory leaves q {q} as a free parameter, any observed pattern of processing difficulty can be accommodated. Specifically, for any difficulty measure d {\mathrm{d}} , one can simply construct a language model whose surprisal is an affine function of it: q → d ​ ( u t ∣ 𝒖 < t ) = def exp ⁡ ( − d ​ ( u t ∣ 𝒖 < t ) ) ∑ u ′ ∈ Σ e exp ⁡ ( − d ​ ( u ′ ∣ 𝒖 < t ) ) . \!{\vec{{q}}_{{\mathrm{d}}}}({u}_{t}\mid{\boldsymbol{u}}_{<t})\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{def}}}{{=}}}\frac{\exp({-{\mathrm{d}}({u}_{t}\mid{\boldsymbol{u}}_{<t})})}{\sum_{{u}^{\prime}\in{{\Sigma}_{\textsc{e}}}}\exp({-{\mathrm{d}}({u}^{\prime}\mid{\boldsymbol{u}}_{<t})})}. The affine formulation with context-dependent b b is therefore the natural statement of the theory. Under mild conditions, explicated in § ˜ 3 , this construction yields a valid language model. 8 8 8 The tautology argument applies more broadly to any theory that defines processing difficulty purely as a function of the language model’s probability distribution. For instance, Hale ’s ( 2003 ) entropy reduction hypothesis—which links processing difficulty to the reduction in entropy over possible parses—faces a similar problem: for any observed pattern of difficulty, one can in principle construct a probability distribution whose entropy reductions match it, though the construction is less direct than in the surprisal case. The consequence is that, without further constraining q {q} , surprisal theory’s claim that difficulty scales with surprisal is vacuous, i.e., it is compatible with every possible pattern of processing difficulty. Of course, proponents of surprisal theory have never claimed that just any language model will do, and neither do I. To escape the tautology, one must restrict attention to a family of language models 𝒬 {\mathcal{Q}} —for example, the set of all probabilistic context-free grammars (PCFGs; Booth and Thompson, 1973 ) —and select a q ∈ 𝒬 {q}\in{\mathcal{Q}} . This is precisely the move Hale ( 2001 ) makes: invoking his Principle 1, which he terms strong competence—a hypothesis originally proposed by Chomsky ( 1965 ) —he restricts 𝒬 {\mathcal{Q}} to the set of PCFGs on rationalist grounds: he believes “the human sentence processing mechanism directly uses rules of grammar in its operation.” The problem is that subsequent empirical work has progressively drifted from such commitments—from PCFGs to recurrent neural networks (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997 ) to transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017 ) —adopting model families whose cognitive relevance is left unjustified, relying instead on the corpus assumption ( § ˜ 1.3 )—the implicit premise that the relevant language model is the very distribution that generated the training corpus, so that fitting that distribution ever more faithfully can only improve predictions of processing difficulty—to do the constraining work that the choice of 𝒬 {\mathcal{Q}} no longer provided—leaving behind only a weaker, implicit assumption that I will call the cognitivist assumption —that q {q} should approximate a theoretical construct p H {p_{\mathrm{H}}} , the comprehender’s internal language model. Levy ( 2008 ) comes closest to making the cognitivist assumption explicit, writing “the cognitive entity of primary interest is the resulting probabilistic [unit] model alone” (p. 1138), and that the choice of grammar “is not a commitment to any particular grammatical formalism as the backbone of sentence comprehension” but rather “a formal means of estimating what expectations about upcoming [units] in a sentence implicitly arise” (p. 1138). Under the cognitivist assumption, surprisal theory reduces to the claim that d ​ ( u t ∣ 𝒖 < t ) = − a ​ log ⁡ p H → ​ ( u t ∣ 𝒖 < t ) + b ​ ( 𝒖 < t ) . \!{\mathrm{d}}({u}_{t}\mid{\boldsymbol{u}}_{<t})=-a\log\vec{{p_{\mathrm{H}}}}({u}_{t}\mid{\boldsymbol{u}}_{<t})+b({\boldsymbol{u}}_{<t}). (3) But this framing exposes that the cognitivist assumption, by itself, does not escape the tautology: without an independent characterization of p H {p_{\mathrm{H}}} that is not grounded in the behavioral data that the field seeks to explain, any pattern of difficulty can be explained by positing a p H {p_{\mathrm{H}}} whose surprisal matches it. 9 9 9 The same structural problem afflicts any theory with an unconstrained latent construct. I call the fact that the falsifiability of surprisal theory requires an externally chosen family of language models 𝒬 {\mathcal{Q}} the grounding problem . Notably, the grounding problem has two parts: first, what family 𝒬 {\mathcal{Q}} should be considered, and second, how should a specific q ∈ 𝒬 {q}\in{\mathcal{Q}} be selected? The first question concerns the structural commitments of the family of language models—whether 𝒬 {\mathcal{Q}} comprises PCFGs, recurrent neural networks, or transformers—while the second concerns the criterion by which q {q} is selected from within 𝒬 {\mathcal{Q}} , e.g., is it fit to a corpus, derived from cognitive principles, or optimized against behavioral data? Surprisal theory itself provides no independent answer to either question—the answer must come from outside the theory. Yet in much of the recent empirical literature on surprisal theory, the choice of 𝒬 {\mathcal{Q}} receives little or no external justification: studies routinely report results for whichever architecture is currently in vogue, e.g., recurrent neural networks or transformers—without arguing that the chosen 𝒬 {\mathcal{Q}} is the right one on cognitive or other theoretical grounds. The implicit assumption is that a better corpus model is a better cognitive model, but this assumption is precisely what is at issue. 1.2 An Analogy from Evolutionary Biology Tautologies are not new in science. An instructive parallel comes from evolutionary biology. Darwin ’s ( 1859 ) principle of natural selection—that heritable traits conferring reproductive advantage spread through a population—is distilled in the slogan survival of the fittest . But if fitness simply means reproductive success, the slogan reduces to “those who reproduce most, reproduce most”—a tautology, not a law of nature. The observation has a long history (Butler, 1882 ; Sinnott et al., 1958 ; Waddington, 1960 ) and was given its most sustained treatment by Peters ( 1976 ) ; Popper famously concluded that natural selection was a “metaphysical research programme” rather than a testable theory (Popper, 1974 ) . The criticism was not that evolution was false, but that its central explanatory construct was defined in terms of the very phenomenon it was meant to explain. The resolution came through what Mills and Beatty ( 1979 ) called the propensity interpretation of fitness; see also Brandon ( 1978 ) . On this view, fitness is not a measure of actual reproductive output but a propensity —a causal tendency, grounded in an organism’s morphology, physiology, and behavior in a given environment, to survive. Under the propensity interpretation, natural selection makes a falsifiable claim: organisms with higher propensities reproduce more than those with lower ones. The key structural feature of the propensity interpretation—and the one I will exploit below—is that it grounds an explanatory construct in physical or structural properties of the organism itself and how it relates to its environment. Crucially, this grounding is independent of the outcome the construct is meant to explain—reproductive success. A propensity interpretation of surprisal theory would require an analogous move: grounding the choice of q {q} in independently observable properties of the comprehender—working memory capacity, parsing strategy, attention allocation policy—rather than in the reading-time data the theory is meant to predict. I discuss concrete proposals along these lines in § ˜ 5 . 1.3 How Surprisal Theory Lost Its Propensity While rarely stated explicitly, I contend that surprisal theory did historically have a propensity interpretation, which I explicate below. Let p C {p_{\mathrm{C}}} denote the data-generating language model of the corpus—the distribution over strings that produced the texts used to estimate q {q} . Just as fitness under the propensity interpretation is grounded in how the organism interacts with its environment—observable physical properties independent of reproductive outcomes— p C {p_{\mathrm{C}}} is grounded in how humans produce text in the wild, observable independently of any processing difficulty measurements. 10 10 10 One might object that the independence is not absolute, i.e.the same cognitive system that produces text also processes it, so p C {p_{\mathrm{C}}} and processing difficulty are not causally unrelated. The dependence may run deeper than mere causal correlation: influential theories of language processing posit shared representations for production and comprehension (Pickering and Garrod, 2004 ; Dell, 1986 ) , in which case p C {p_{\mathrm{C}}} is not independent of p H {p_{\mathrm{H}}} but rather a noisy-channel reflection of it. If production and comprehension share the same underlying language model, the corpus assumption and the cognitivist assumption would collapse into one—an identification that, if correct, would simplify the grounding problem considerably. The point, for present purposes, is that p C {p_{\mathrm{C}}} can be estimated without recourse to reading-time data, which is sufficient for the propensity move to go through. I concede, however, that the relationship between production and comprehension distributions deserves more careful treatment than I am able to give it here. To state it more concisely, the assumption that has anchored two decades of empirical work in surprisal theory—call it the corpus assumption —is that q = p C {q}={p_{\mathrm{C}}} . Under the corpus assumption, surprisal theory claims the following d ​ ( u t ∣ 𝒖 < t ) = − a ​ log ⁡ p → C ​ ( u t ∣ 𝒖 < t ) + b ​ ( 𝒖 < t ) . \!{\mathrm{d}}({u}_{t}\mid{\boldsymbol{u}}_{<t})=-a\log{\vec{{p}}_{\mathrm{C}}}({u}_{t}\mid{\boldsymbol{u}}_{<t})+b({\boldsymbol{u}}_{<t}). (4) One wrinkle is that p C {p_{\mathrm{C}}} is not known. However, it can be approximated by estimating a language model from a corpus of texts assumed to have been sampled from p C {p_{\mathrm{C}}} . The corpus assumption led to two concrete payoffs. First, it made finding a q {q} to experiment with in practice approachable: one can estimate a language model q {q} from a corpus and treat it as an approximation to p C {p_{\mathrm{C}}} . Second, under maximum-likelihood estimation, the corpus assumption entails what I call the scaling implication —as estimation improves, a model q {q} should asymptotically yield surprisal values that better correlate with processing difficulty. This implication is a direct consequence of the corpus assumption, as I formally argue in § ˜ 4 , and forces surprisal theory to make a falsifiable prediction. In practice, however, the corpus assumption has seldom been enforced in pure form. Studies routinely compare many language models by their fit to behavioral data and report the best-fitting configurations (e.g., Goodkind and Bicknell, 2018 ; Wilcox et al., 2023 ; Oh and Schuler, 2023 ) , so that subsequent work, in adopting those models, implicitly conditions the choice of q {q} on the very data the theory is meant to explain; hyperparameter and checkpoint selection introduce a logical dependence, albeit a mild one. At the extreme, Kiegeland et al. ( 2024 ) fine-tune a language model on reading times directly; I return to the status of this strategy in § ˜ 4 . 11 11 11 In the same vein, Yoshida et al. ( 2026 ) fine-tune neural language models on garden-path reading times, yielding an “existence proof” of a language model whose surprisal reproduces garden-path effects that off-the-shelf models notoriously underestimate—and they note that such constructibility may render surprisal theory “unfalsifiable in practice.” Their empirical construction is the practical counterpart of the formal one in § 3 ; notably, however, their fine-tuned models still fail to reproduce memory-based effects such as the subject–object relative-clause asymmetry, showing that the family reachable by fine-tuning in practice is not yet universal—a contingent bound on flexibility that, as the formal argument shows, cannot be relied upon in principle. On my reading of the literature, two decades of empirical work implicitly operated under the corpus assumption. And, for most of that time, the results suggested that contextual surprisal derived from larger language models did in fact correlate more strongly with a variety of behavioral measurements, e.g., self-paced reading times (Smith and Levy, 2013 ; Wilcox et al., 2023 ) , eye-tracking measures (Boston et al., 2008 ; Demberg and Keller, 2008 ) , and neural signals (Frank et al., 2015 ; Giulianelli et al., 2024 ) across languages and model architectures—from probabilistic context-free grammars to echo state networks ( cf. Jaeger, 2001 ; Frank and Bod, 2011 ) , long short-term memory networks ( cf. Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997 ; Goodkind and Bicknell, 2018 ) , and large pretrained transformers ( cf. Vaswani et al., 2017 ; Wilcox et al., 2020 ) . With each architectural shift, the cognitive commitments implicit in the choice of 𝒬 {\mathcal{Q}} became less transparent: a context-free grammar commits to a linguistically motivated 𝒬 {\mathcal{Q}} (Hale, 2001 ) , but for a neural language model the constraints on q {q} are opaque—even though the family may be surprisingly restricted. 12 12 12 Yang et al. ( 2026 ) characterize the family that autoregressive transformer-based language models can compute. Under fixed precision (Li and Cotterell, 2025 ) , it corresponds to a sub regular family. This implies that transformer-based language models correspond to very big probabilistic finite-state automata, which are less expressive than PCFGs in terms of the Chomsky hierarchy. Bergsträßer et al. ( 2026 ) show, moreover, that transformers are an inherently succinct representation of such automata—they can encode PFSAs that would require exponentially more states if represented directly. Recently, however, a growing body of evidence appears to falsify the scaling implication—and, with it, the corpus assumption specifically, not surprisal theory per se . Oh and Schuler ( 2023 ) first reported that the correlation between surprisal and reading times improves as transformers grow larger, but only up to a point—beyond which it degrades as models become better approximations to p C {p_{\mathrm{C}}} . 13 13 13 Kuribayashi et al. ( 2025 ) argue that this degradation is an artifact of evaluating only final-layer representations: middle layers of larger models retain strong alignment with human reading times. Relatedly, Tsipidi et al. ( 2026 ) find that early-layer representations outperform surprisal itself in predicting early-pass reading measures across five languages. However, this does not rescue the scaling implication, which concerns the model’s closeness to p C {p_{\mathrm{C}}} . This finding has since been replicated and extended. Oh et al. ( 2024 ) confirmed the inverse relationship across four language model families and four reading corpora, arguing that word frequency explains much of the degradation. Lin and Schuler ( 2025 ) demonstrate that the same inverse trend appears for fMRI-based neural measures, extending the finding beyond latency-based reading times. Finally, Oh et al. ( 2025 ) claim to have ruled out data leakage as an explanation, showing that the inverse relationship persists even with models trained on data from which reading-time corpora have been removed. My argument relies on these findings being correct, but I acknowledge that the case is not fully closed: one might argue that the degradation reflects a mismatch between the corpora used to train current language models (predominantly web text) and the cognitively relevant distribution, rather than a failure of the corpus assumption per se . 14 14 14 If one considers a corpus of conversational speech rather than web text, the scaling implication might still hold for models trained on that corpus. Distinguishing “no data-generating distribution p C {p_{\mathrm{C}}} yields the right q {q} ” from “the right p C {p_{\mathrm{C}}} has simply not been identified” is an open empirical question that the formal argument of this paper does not resolve. 2 Formal Preliminaries Alphabets, strings, and language models.
